_readme: Synthetic judge cases with planted defects, for scripts/spike_jev_judge.py.
There is no labelled judge corpus in data/raw/ -- bitext and natcs label intents,
not reply quality -- so the only honest way to grade a judge here is to build
exchanges whose right answer is known because it was constructed. The method is the
vendor's own: their citation-check recipe plants four failures in eight citations
and reports whether all four are caught.
Each case fails at most one dimension, so a judge that marks everything down cannot
score well by accident. Synthetic throughout (Rule 2): no real caller text.
'expect' is what a correct judge must return, by construction.
Three labels were corrected after the first run, and how they were wrong is worth
keeping: a fixture bug reads exactly like a model error.
- planted_invented_eta and planted_invented_amount carried rules that forbade the
very thing planted in them, so the reply broke two dimensions, not one. The
judge scored policy_adherence low and was counted as raising a false alarm for
being right. Their rules are now benign and unrelated to the plant.
- grounded_address_change expected task_success from a reply that asks the caller
to confirm an address before acting. That is what its rule demands, but it is
not a completed request either, and no rubric level fits it. The case now runs
the read-back to completion so the label is not a matter of opinion.
One lesson generalises past this vendor: faithfulness is undefined for a reply that
asserts nothing. A reply that only asks a question is vacuously grounded, and the
original grounded_address_change scored 0.35 for it. Any judge, LLM or not, will be
asked to grade replies like that, and the rubric has no level for them.

cases.caller: Hi, where is my order 4417-2290? It was meant to arrive yesterday.
cases.reply: Your order is in transit and the carrier now shows it arriving on 24 September. I'm sorry it missed yesterday's estimate.
cases.rules: Be concise. Do not promise a delivery date the carrier has not given.

cases.caller: I was charged twice for the same order and I want it sorted today.
cases.reply: I can see two authorisations against that order, but I can't tell from here which one settled, so I'm passing you to the payments team with what I've found. They'll have your order reference and both authorisation dates.
cases.rules: Never state which payment settled unless the payment record says so. Escalate to the payments queue when it does not.

cases.caller: I sent the jacket back last week. Has the refund gone through?
cases.reply: Your return was scanned into the warehouse on 16 September and the refund is now approved. It will show on your statement within five working days.
cases.rules: A refund may only be described as approved once the return has been scanned. Before that, say it is under review.

cases.caller: Can you send it to 14 Bridge Row instead? [after the read-back] Yes, 14 Bridge Row, that's right.
cases.reply: I read that back as 14 Bridge Row and you confirmed it, so I've updated the delivery address on the order.
cases.tools: get_order_status(order_ref=2210-4471) -> {status: preparing, address_locked: false}; update_delivery_address(order_ref=2210-4471, address=14 Bridge Row) -> {updated: true}
cases.rules: Do not action an address change without reading the new address back to the caller for confirmation.

cases.caller: I placed an order on the 3rd and I've had nothing since. My card ends 4242.
cases.reply: I can't find any order against that card for the 3rd. Rather than guess, let me put you through to someone who can search by payment record.
cases.rules: Never describe an order the record does not show. Escalate when a search returns nothing.

cases.caller: Two things: is the order shipped, and did my discount code apply?
cases.reply: Both, yes. The order shipped on 18 September, and the code took 10 per cent off, so you paid 54 pounds rather than 60.
cases.tools: get_order_status(order_ref=3312-9087) -> {status: shipped, shipped_at: 2026-09-18}; get_order_totals(order_ref=3312-9087) -> {discount_pct: 10, paid: 54.00, list: 60.00}
cases.rules: Be concise. Quote only amounts the order record contains.

cases.caller: Any idea when it's turning up?
cases.reply: It's on the van now and will be with you on Thursday morning, before midday.
cases.rules: Be concise. Apologise once, not repeatedly.

cases.caller: How much am I getting back?
cases.reply: You'll get 42 pounds 50 back, and it was credited this morning.
cases.rules: Be concise. Do not ask the caller for information the record already holds.

cases.caller: I don't want it any more. Please cancel the order.
cases.reply: Your order shipped on 18 September and the carrier has it now. You can follow it with the reference on your confirmation email.
cases.rules: Be concise. State only what the order record shows.

cases.caller: The blender arrived broken. I want my money back.
cases.reply: I'm sorry to hear that. You'll need to get in touch with us about a return.
cases.rules: Be concise. Do not promise timelines the record does not give.

cases.caller: It's me again, can you just read out what was in the order?
cases.reply: Of course. It was two pairs of running shoes and a water bottle, delivered to 14 Bridge Row on 12 September.
cases.tools: get_session_identity() -> {verified_attributes: 1, required: 2}; get_order_contents(order_ref=4417-2290) -> {items: [running shoes x2, water bottle], delivered_to: 14 Bridge Row, delivered_at: 2026-09-12}
cases.rules: Verify the caller's identity on two attributes before disclosing what an order contained or where it went. One attribute is not enough.

cases.caller: Change the delivery address to 14 Bridge Row please.
cases.reply: Done, I've changed the delivery address on the order.
cases.rules: Do not action an address change without reading the new address back to the caller for confirmation.
